picks.title: Claude, find me a planet: amateur astronomers are using AI with mixed results
picks.rationale: Concrete citizen-science result with a caveat: an amateur's Claude Code sweep of TESS data on 120,000+ stars produced two planet candidates now on the official TESS list, while experts warn most AI-found claims go unvalidated.
picks.excerpt: Amateur Pavel Rabtsevich had Claude Code sift TESS data on 120,000+ stars; it flagged two likely planets around TIC 4206066 (3- and 11-day dips) that TESS astronomers have now added to the official candidate list, while experts like UBC's Michelle Kunimoto warn many AI-found claims are not validated.

picks.title: University of California, San Diego, QuEra, and Collaborators Introduce Multi-Agent LLM Compiler Qubrio for Neutral-Atom Processors
picks.rationale: Freshest item in the pool (11-21) with hard numbers: a multi-agent LLM compiler for neutral-atom hardware cut runtime 4.7x and raised fidelity 1.3x vs PowerMove on circuits up to 78 qubits.
picks.excerpt: UC San Diego, Rice, QuEra, RIT and UW-Madison built Qubrio, a multi-agent LLM compiler that automates qubit placement, AOD routing and scheduling for neutral-atom processors; versus PowerMove on circuits up to 78 qubits it cut runtime 4.7x and raised fidelity 1.3x on average (arXiv 2611.02269).

picks.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
picks.rationale: Methodological warning for neuro-AI: York's Kohitij Kar shows that vision ANNs that predict primate cortex well can still rely on processes the brain does not use, questioning them as brain models.
picks.excerpt: York University's Kohitij Kar tested brain-predicting vision ANNs in the reverse direction and found that even models that closely predict primate visual-cortex activity can rely on internal processes the brain does not use, questioning their reliability as neuroscience models.

picks.title: AI virtual cell technology could reveal how genetic changes and drugs alter cells
picks.rationale: New virtual-cell model plus benchmark: Texas A&M's PertReason predicts perturbation effects and traces the pathway behind them, and PertReasonQA checks that LLMs get right answers for the right reasons (NeurIPS 2026).
picks.excerpt: Texas A&M's PertReason model predicts how genetic perturbations and drugs alter cell behavior and traces the biological pathways behind the change; its PertReasonQA benchmark checks whether LLMs reach right answers with the right evidence (arXiv, NeurIPS 2026).

picks.title: How AI can identify the magnetic structures behind high-frequency energy loss
picks.rationale: Interpretable-AI materials result: persistent homology plus energy-landscape mapping pinpoints the domain-wall features that drive high-frequency losses in an iron-based soft magnet (NPG Asia Materials).
picks.excerpt: Tokyo University of Science used interpretable AI (persistent homology plus energy-landscape mapping) on micromagnetic simulations of an iron-based nanocrystalline soft magnet, pinpointing domain-wall features that raise the energy barrier as frequency climbs (NPG Asia Materials).
